{{Short description|Represents a function with diffusion properties useful in cryptography}}
An '''MDS matrix''' ('''maximum distance separable''') is a [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] representing a function with certain [[diffusion (cryptography)|diffusion]] properties that have useful applications in [[cryptography]]. Technically, an <math>m \times n</math> matrix <math>A</math> over a [[finite field]] <math>K</math> is an MDS matrix if it is the [[transformation matrix]] of a [[linear transformation]] <math>f(x) = Ax</math> from <math>K^n</math> to <math>K^m</math> such that no two different <math>(m + n)</math>-tuples of the form <math>(x, f(x))</math> coincide in <math>n</math> or more components.
Equivalently, the set of all <math>(m + n)</math>-tuples <math>(x, f(x))</math> is an [[Maximum distance separable code|MDS code]], i.e., a [[linear code]] that reaches the [[Singleton bound]].

Let <math>\tilde A = \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{I}_n \\ \hline \mathrm{A} \end{pmatrix}</math> be the matrix obtained by joining the [[identity matrix]] <math>\mathrm{I}_n</math> to <math>A</math>. Then a necessary and sufficient condition for a matrix <math>A</math> to be MDS is that every possible <math>n \times n</math> [[submatrix]] obtained by removing <math>m</math> rows from <math>\tilde A</math> is [[non-singular matrix|non-singular]]. This is also equivalent to the following: all the sub-determinants of the matrix <math>A</math> are non-zero. Then a binary matrix <math>A</math> (namely over the field with two elements) is never MDS unless it has only one row or only one column with all components <math>1</math>.

[[Reed–Solomon code]]s have the MDS property and are frequently used to obtain the MDS matrices used in cryptographic algorithms.

[[Serge Vaudenay]] suggested using MDS matrices in [[cryptographic primitive]]s to produce what he called ''multipermutations'', not-necessarily linear functions with this same property.<ref>{{Citation |last=Vaudenay |first=Serge |chapter=On the need for multipermutations: Cryptanalysis of MD4 and SAFER |date=1995 |title=Fast Software Encryption |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=1008 |pages=286–297 |editor-last=Preneel |editor-first=Bart |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |doi=10.1007/3-540-60590-8_22 |isbn=978-3-540-60590-4|doi-access=free }}</ref> These functions have what he called ''perfect diffusion'': changing <math>t</math> of the inputs changes at least <math>m - t + 1</math> of the outputs. He showed how to exploit imperfect diffusion to [[cryptanalysis|cryptanalyze]] functions that are not multipermutations.

MDS matrices are used for diffusion in such [[block cipher]]s as [[Advanced Encryption Standard|AES]], [[SHARK]], [[Square (cipher)|Square]], [[Twofish]], [[Anubis (cipher)|Anubis]], [[KHAZAD]], [[Manta (cipher)|Manta]], [[Hierocrypt]], [[Kalyna (cipher)|Kalyna]], [[Camellia (cipher)|Camellia]] and [[HADESMiMC]], and in the [[stream cipher]] [[MUGI]] and the [[cryptographic hash function]] [[Whirlpool (cryptography)|Whirlpool]], [[Poseidon (cryptography)|Poseidon]].
